slides.title: Media and information technology
slides.notes:
PC00 · Title
[The arrival loop runs while the room settles: the ribbon drifts and the three chips pulse.]
Welcome — this is a working session of sorts: forty minutes on information literacy, and the habits underneath it.
▶ Click: the fern.

slides.title: Recursion
slides.notes:
B01 · Recursion
Nobody drew this fern.
A computer took four tiny rules and fed each answer back in as the next question, over and over, and the leaf appeared.
Zoom in and you find the whole fern again. And again.
That's recursion: the same rule, applied to its own output.

▶ Click: the rule comes out of the fern.

slides.title: Same rule
slides.notes:
B02a · Same rule (plays, then holds on the lungs)
Watch the rule underneath the fern.
[As it becomes rivers] The same rule makes a coastline: rivers splitting into smaller rivers, and every bay with smaller bays inside it.
[As it turns into lungs] Turn it over and it's inside you: a pair of lungs. One tube splitting in two, and again, and again.

▶ Click: a brain cell.

slides.title: Same rule, part 2
slides.notes:
B02b · A brain cell
And it's the cell you're thinking with right now. It branches the same way, gathers signals, and passes one on.
A second thought is that loop on purpose: your own thinking, fed back in.

▶ Click: Now, AI.

slides.title: Now, AI
slides.notes:
B02c · Now, AI
Now, AI.
It's loosely modelled on those cells: layers of simple connections.
It makes a guess, checks how far off it was, adjusts its connections, and goes round again.
The same rule, applied to its own output.

▶ Click: the turn.

slides.title: The turn
slides.notes:
B03 · The turn
If the machine recurses on knowledge, the value isn't in knowing.
[Pause. Let it land. This slide is meant to be still.]
And it's not just me saying that.

▶ Click: Seymour Papert.

slides.title: Watershed
slides.notes:
B04 · Watershed
[Let the top-left Lineage card grow and flip into the MIT paper. Begin the next concept once the poster has opened and its quote arrives.]
In August, MIT's president, Sally Kornbluth, wrote to her whole community that AI in education is a watershed moment for MIT.
And she quoted her own AI committee: responding to it is not an optional exercise.
Their report points to three things: education that is AI-aware, people and community, and continuous reflection.

▶ Click: what MIT's students say.

slides.title: Three numbers
slides.notes:
B05a · Three numbers
Here's what MIT's own undergraduates said, in a survey by The Tech, their student paper, late last year.
46 per cent use an AI chatbot every day.
90 per cent worry they're becoming over-reliant on it.

▶ Click: the third number.

slides.title: Removing the barrier
slides.notes:
B05b · The third number
And only 25 per cent think MIT is preparing them to use AI.
[Pause.]
That's MIT. It's worth asking how our students would answer.

▶ Click: so what do we teach?

slides.title: States
slides.notes:
PC02 · States
Good thinking has conditions. Habits of mind shape how we approach information, AI, reading and creativity.
We call those conditions states. Everything today hangs off that claim: literacy work is state work.
▶ Click: the portal into section one.

slides.title: Section 1: Thinking routines
slides.notes:
PC03 · Thinking Routines
Three stops: wellbeing, executive function, and AI as a thought partner.
Wellbeing comes first on purpose — before sources and search strings, the conditions that make evaluation possible.
▶ Click: wellbeing.

slides.title: Wellbeing first
slides.notes:
PC04 · Wellbeing first
Sleep. Attention. Emotions. Digital balance.
Parents often expect information literacy to begin with evaluating sources. I'd argue it begins earlier: in a state where thoughtful evaluation is possible.
▶ Click: executive function.

slides.title: Executive function
slides.notes:
PC05 · Executive function
Technology is most powerful when it helps students manage their thinking — not replace it.
Note-taking systems, calendars and task lists, timers and time boxes, reading workflows. This is the Sarah Ward territory: executive function, not gadgets.
The core skill: organizing attention.
▶ Click: Flint.

PC06a · Flint — the worry
Here's the use of AI that rightly worries parents: AI as replacement.
Write this for me. Give me the answer. Do the thinking.
▶ Click: the other column.

PC06b · Flint — the partner
AI as thought partner. Help me improve this. Help me understand. Extend my thinking.
Same tool — the habit decides which column a student lives in.
▶ Click: the bridge.

slides.title: From thinking to creating
slides.notes:
PC07 · From thinking to creating
[Let the navy field sit for a beat.]
Creativity grows from strong thinking routines — reflection, questioning, reading, idea capture, conversation with AI.
▶ Click: section two.

slides.title: Section 2: Creativity
slides.notes:
PC08 · Creativity
Strong creativity is not the opposite of structure. It grows from the routines we just walked through.
▶ Click: reading.

PC09a · Why reading matters
Parents can see reading as competing with technology. I'd frame it as the original creativity technology.
Vocabulary. Background knowledge. Imagination and empathy. Ideas that connect. Every one of them feeds both human creativity and AI use.
▶ Click: the payoff.

PC09b · Ideas worth remixing
AI can remix ideas — students still need ideas worth remixing.
▶ Click: what to put in the diet.

slides.title: Better information diets
slides.notes:
PC10 · Better information diets
The point isn't these specific names — Sooth.fyi, The Economist, long-form journalism, books and newsletters.
The point is: information literacy depends on the quality of the information we consume.
▶ Click: the turn.

slides.title: Better questions
slides.notes:
PC11 · Better questions
We often worry whether students know the right answers.
What matters more: do they learn to ask better questions?
▶ Click: the loop.

slides.title: The loop
slides.notes:
PC12 · The loop
Learn, think, create, question — repeat. Those habits are recursive.
Every day they shape how students learn, think, create, and participate in an AI-rich world.
▶ Click: thanks.

slides.title: Thank you
slides.notes:
PC13 · Thank you
Questions welcome. The QR links to these slides and the resources once they're posted.
